title: Empty the boat (366–372)
hook: empty this boat and it will sail lightly; no meditation without wisdom, no wisdom without meditation

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhikkhu, a monk who lives on what is given, and your line: restraint is good.

Picture a small wooden boat on a river after a storm. It's riding low, sluggish, barely moving. Water has been coming in all night, and now it sloshes around your ankles. Row as hard as you like; a boat full of water just won't go. What it needs first isn't more effort. It needs someone to pick up a bucket and start bailing. Plenty of days get rowed with the boat half full: old worries, old resentments, a list that keeps getting carried.
screen: `A BOAT RIDING LOW.` → `ROWING HARDER WON'T HELP.` → `PICK UP THE BUCKET.`

segments.voice: The mendicant chapter goes on with the monk's life. A monk who gets little but doesn't look down on it, one verse says, is praised even by the gods. A monk who lives in kindness, in metta, with faith in the teaching, reaches the place of peace. Then verse three hundred sixty-nine, in Max Müller's English: "O Bhikshu, empty this boat! if emptied, it will go quickly; having cut off passion and hatred thou wilt go to Nirvana." The boat, the old commentators say, is this life, this body and mind. The water is wrong thinking, especially greed and hatred, seeping in. Bail them out, and the boat rides light and fast toward the far shore. The river and the far shore are old pictures in this tradition; the next verse speaks of the one who has crossed the flood. Then, at the end of this passage, comes one of the most quoted verses in the book: there is no meditation without wisdom, and no wisdom without meditation. The one who has both is close to nirvana. In Pali the two words are jhana, deep meditative absorption, and panna, wisdom or understanding. They need each other. Sitting still without understanding can become a pleasant nap. Understanding without stillness stays in the head, an idea about the boat. Together they're the bucket and the arm that lifts it. So emptying the boat isn't just stopping thoughts. It's seeing clearly what's come in, and letting it go overboard, one bucket at a time.
screen: `THE MONK WHO LIVES IN KINDNESS.` · `EMPTY THE BOAT, IT GOES QUICKLY.` · `GREED AND HATRED, SEEPING IN.` · `NO JHANA WITHOUT PANNA.` · then, large: `EMPTY THE BOAT.`

segments.voice: Imagine yourself in a small boat on a calm river, the water around your ankles one worry you've carried today; name it simply, scoop it up in a bucket, and pour it over the side to drift downstream. If it seeps back in, that's fine, boats leak; just bail again, gently. Then notice the boat sitting a little higher, and let the breath carry you.
Paññā. Wisdom: bail out greed and hatred, and the boat of this life sails lightly, since wisdom and meditation work together.
Your line: one bucket at a time. Emptied, the boat goes quickly. That's day two hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often quote verse 372 to explain that calm meditation and wisdom are trained together; many meditation traditions pair a practice of stillness with a practice of insight.

fork.setup: your boat is riding low and barely moving. what do you do first?
options: pick up a bucket and bail.
fork.reveal: verse 369: empty this boat, and it will go quickly. bail out greed and hatred first; then the rowing works.

original.note: Pali paññā: wisdom; verse 372 says there is no wisdom without meditation (jhāna).

trapdoor: what you thought: 'empty the boat' means empty your mind of all thoughts.
what it means: bail out greed and hatred, so this life rides lightly toward peace.
what a scholar hears: verse 372, 'natthi jhanam apannassa, panna natthi ajhayato', pairs jhana and panna; the commentary reads the boat as the body and the water as wrong thoughts.
